title: Start the Work Before You Get the Assignment
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article argues that the strongest way to win an assignment, contract, or job is to demonstrate the work itself rather than merely propose to do it. It points to teams that win more competitive bids by delivering a piece of actual design or analysis up front, arguing this signals confidence and commitment that a written proposal can't match. The same principle is extended to interviews, contrasting a candidate who arrives with prepared questions against one who arrives with workable solutions. The piece acknowledges the real risk — investing unpaid effort that may never be rewarded, or having ideas taken without credit — but concludes the payoff in differentiation is usually worth that risk.
points: Delivering a piece of actual work or design before being awarded a contract is presented as more persuasive than any written proposal, because it demonstrates rather than promises commitment.
The same logic is applied to job interviews: a candidate offering workable solutions outperforms one who arrives only with prepared questions.
The piece names the real downside honestly — unpaid effort that may never be compensated, or ideas being used without credit — rather than presenting the tactic as risk-free.
The closing framing, "commitment and resolve are best displayed by illustration and not suggestion," positions demonstrated work as the sharpest differentiator available.
quotes: They have the biggest soft spot for those who go the extra step and prove they are willing to do whatever it takes to get the job done.
Examine teams that win more bake-offs and requests for proposals than others, and you will often find a team that does more than make a proposal.
Offering solutions rather than merely proposing to do so often wins the day.
Great leaders have a strong bias for action and reward it when they see it in others.
Beginning the work before it is actually requested or awarded is a risky move because it can mean investing in something that never materializes.
They know that commitment and resolve are best displayed by illustration and not suggestion.
